358.title: When a neighbor's cup breaks
358.hook: when someone else's cup breaks we say "these things happen," so say it of your own (Enchiridion 26)
358.tomorrow: A target isn't set up to be missed
358.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat their own setbacks the way they would a friend's, using the same calm words they would readily offer someone else.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was obol, the small coin that buys the lettuce. Your line was I kept the coin.

A friend texts: I dented my car backing out of the garage. Your reply takes four seconds. Oh no! Happens to everyone. Is anyone hurt? That's what matters. Wise, calm, kind. A week later you dent your own car backing out of your own garage, and for the next hour you're a different person. Idiot. How could I. This always happens to me. Same kind of dent, same kind of morning. Section twenty-six of the handbook says the wisdom you need was in that four-second text.
screen: `A FRIEND'S DENTED CAR.` → `HAPPENS TO EVERYONE.` → `THEN IT'S YOUR CAR.`

segments.voice: What nature intends, Epictetus says, we can learn from the cases where we all agree. Not from arguments, but from our own easy answers about other people's troubles. When someone else's servant breaks a cup, people are quick to say: these things happen. So, he says, when your own cup breaks, be the same as you were when the other one broke. That's all. Borrow your own good advice. Then he carries it further, gently but firmly. When someone else's child or spouse dies, everyone says: that's the human lot. But when it's one's own, right away it's: oh, poor me, how wretched. We ought to remember, he says, how we felt when we heard the same news about others. Here it's worth slowing down, because this is a hard line to hear. Epictetus asks a great deal: the same steadiness for your own loss as for a stranger's. Not every reader will follow him that far, and nobody here is asked to. But the part anyone can use is narrower. It's the doubled suffering, the sense that this, unlike everyone else's, shouldn't have happened, that the world has made an exception of you. Often the wise, steady friend who knows exactly what to say about broken cups is already in the room. It's you, talking to someone else. The trick is to turn around and say it to yourself, with the same warmth. It's strangely close to the old rule about loving your neighbor as yourself, only running backward. Treat yourself, for a moment, as you'd treat your neighbor. These things happen. To them. To you.

Let your words for them come, kind and steady. Then turn them around and say them to yourself, in the same tone: these things happen.

359.title: A target isn't set up to be missed
359.hook: evil isn't built into nature, any more than a target is set up to be missed (Enchiridion 27)
359.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat mistakes as misses rather than proof that the good is out of reach, and choose a specific good to aim at each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was cup. When anyone's cup breaks, a neighbor's or your own, your line was these things happen.

At an archery range, the targets stand in a row: straw bales, painted rings, a gold circle in the middle. Some arrows land in the gold. Many land in the outer rings, the grass, the fence behind. But nobody hangs a target hoping it will be missed. It exists to be hit. The misses are real, sometimes lots of them, but they aren't what the target is for. Section twenty-seven of the handbook is one puzzling sentence built on that picture.
screen: `AN ARCHERY RANGE.` → `ARROWS IN THE GRASS.` → `NOBODY HANGS A TARGET TO BE MISSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence. Just as a target isn't set up in order to be missed, Epictetus says, so the nature of evil doesn't arise in the world. That's all. No example, no explanation. Now the honest part: readers still argue about this line, and nobody can be sure exactly what he meant. Two readings have lasted. One, from the ancient commentator Simplicius and others: the world is ordered toward the good, the way a target is set up to be hit. Evil isn't one of its built-in parts. It's a missing, a falling short, real but not the point. Two, a more practical reading: in the world outside us, nothing is truly evil, because for a Stoic the only real evil is a bad choice in a person's own will. Either way, the mark is there to be aimed at. The Greek for target is skopos, the mark an archer fixes the eye on. The picture doesn't deny the misses; the grass behind a range is full of arrows. It says they aren't why the target is there. A miss only counts as a miss because there's a mark to measure it by. Whatever the metaphysics, the practice is simple. A miss doesn't mean the target was a lie. Yesterday's sharp word, last week's broken promise: arrows in the grass. The gold is still there. Pick up another arrow. Aim at the good.
screen: `NOT SET UP TO BE MISSED.` · `TWO READINGS, NO CERTAINTY.` · `SKOPOS: THE MARK.` · `PICK UP ANOTHER ARROW.` · then, large: `AIM AT THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Picture a target, the gold circle clear in the middle, and put one small, specific good in it: a patient answer, a finished task, a kind word to someone who's hard to like. Let one recent miss lie in the grass without picking it up to examine it. Then breathe in, and draw back an imaginary bow toward the gold.
Skopos. The Greek word for a target, the mark an archer fixes the eye on; misses are real, but they aren't the point. Today's word.
Your line: aim at the good. Misses land in the grass; the target stays. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

360.title: Who handed you over?
360.hook: you'd be furious if someone handed your body to a stranger, so why hand your mind to anyone who insults you? (Enchiridion 28)
360.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners notice when another person's words have taken over their thoughts, and deliberately return their attention to their own judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was skopos, the target. A miss is real, but the mark is there to be hit. Your line was aim at the good.

You're at a bus stop when the person next to you takes your house keys out of your hand and gives them to a stranger walking past. Take care of these. You'd be on your feet, chasing the stranger down the block. Nobody gets to hand over your keys. A different afternoon: a stranger in a comment section says something nasty about you. For the next three hours, that stranger decides what you think about, how you feel, what you say at dinner. You handed them the keys yourself.
screen: `YOUR KEYS, HANDED TO A STRANGER.` → `A NASTY COMMENT.` → `THREE HOURS, GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: In section twenty-eight of the Enchiridion, Epictetus says that if someone handed your body over to whoever happened to meet you, you'd be indignant. But you hand over your own mind to anyone you happen to meet, so that if they abuse you, it's shaken and thrown into confusion. Aren't you ashamed of that? He's blunt. The word for mind here is gnome: your judgment, your way of thinking, the place you decide from. This differs from the insult, a little over a week ago. That day was about the moment of sting, and a breath between the sting and the reply. This is about ownership: who is allowed into the control room? A stranger can say anything; that isn't up to you. But whether their words get the keys, whether they sit in your mind all afternoon and steer, Epictetus thinks that part is yours to decide. Keeping the keys doesn't mean never being affected. A cruel word will land; you're not stone. It means noticing when you've started running someone else's script: the replay in the shower, the imaginary argument on the commute, the urge to check if they've said more. When you catch it, ask his question, a little amused at yourself: who handed you over? Then, gently, take the keys back. My mind is mine. There's something dignified in that. Not proud. Just a person who knows where their own house is, and doesn't leave the door open for anyone who happens by.

segments.voice: Notice who is in your mind right now besides you: someone from an argument, a voice from the news, a comment from this morning. Picture them at the desk inside your head, steering, and don't fight them; just thank them, walk them to the door, and close it. Then take your seat again, with your own breath and your own quiet.

361.title: Count the cost first
361.hook: before you begin anything, look at what comes first and what follows, like an athlete before the games (Enchiridion 29)
361.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners, before taking on something new, picture its demands and setbacks in detail and only then decide whether to begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was gnome, your judgment, the place you decide from. Your line was my mind is mine.
screen: `WHO HANDED YOU OVER? — MY MIND IS MINE.`

segments.voice: New running shoes, still in the box. A water bottle with the hours printed down the side. A plan taped to the fridge. A few weeks later, the shoes are in the closet. The wanting didn't stop. The plan was all beginning and no middle: nobody pictured the five-forty alarm in the dark, the sore knees, the Thursday that didn't feel like it. Section twenty-nine of the handbook is about that missing middle, and it uses an athlete to show it.
screen: `NEW SHOES, STILL IN THE BOX.` → `A FEW WEEKS LATER: THE CLOSET.` → `ALL BEGINNING, NO MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: In every undertaking, Epictetus says, look at what comes before it and what follows from it, and only then set about it. Otherwise you'll start eagerly, and later, when the hard parts show up, you'll give up in shame. Then the athlete. You want to win at Olympia? So do I, he says; it's a fine thing. But look at what comes first. A strict routine, eating on a schedule, no sweets, training at set hours in heat and cold, no cold water and no wine when you're told not to, handing yourself to the trainer as to a doctor. Then in the contest you may dislocate a wrist, twist an ankle, swallow a lot of dust, take a beating, and after all that, lose. Skip the counting, he says, and you'll be like children who play wrestlers, then gladiators, then trumpeters, then actors, trying everything and finishing nothing. Weigh it all, and if you still want it, go ahead. The same picture appears in the Gospel of Luke, about following Jesus, in the King James words: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?" A different teacher, a different calling, the same sitting down before you start. Epictetus isn't trying to scare anyone off. People who have already seen the middle are better placed to get through it.

362.title: What the role asks
362.hook: duties are measured by relationships: father, brother, neighbor (Enchiridion 30)
362.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often think through their roles, as child, parent, friend, neighbor or worker, and ask what each one asks of them, rather than what the other person has earned.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Olympia, and the athlete who counts the whole training before signing up. Your line was first, what follows.

A student comes to Epictetus with a complaint that sounds airtight. My father is a bad father. Surely that changes what I owe him. People still bring that question to therapists, to clergy, to friends at two in the morning. The handbook's thirtieth section answers it with a short reply that has been argued over ever since. It doesn't start with feelings, or with fairness. It starts with a relationship, and asks what that relationship, on its own, asks of you.
screen: `MY FATHER IS A BAD FATHER.` → `SURELY THAT CHANGES THINGS?` → `WHAT THE ROLE ASKS.`

segments.voice: Duties, Epictetus says, are measured by relationships. Is he a father? Then the role asks you to take care of him and give way to him. But he's a bad father, says the student. Epictetus answers: were you tied by nature to a good father? No. To a father. Then the brother. Your brother treats you unjustly. Keep your own place toward him, Epictetus says. Don't watch what he is doing; watch what you must do to keep your own choices in line with nature. And his usual hinge: no one can harm you unless you allow it. The Stoics called a fitting act kathēkon, what's appropriate for this creature, in this place, in this relationship. The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says Zeno, the school's founder, first used the term. Later Cicero turned it into Latin as officium, and wrote a whole book, On Duties, around it. That Latin word is the far ancestor of the English word office, a post with things you're expected to do. The method: you'll find the duty of a neighbor, a citizen, a general, Epictetus says, if you get used to looking at the relationship itself. Ask what am I to this person, and the next step usually shows up. One honest caution. Epictetus wrote that a son should bear even blows from his father, in a world that took that for granted. Many modern readers of the Stoics add plainly that no role asks anyone to stay in danger, and protecting yourself is also a duty. What the chapter keeps is narrower: their failure doesn't erase your part.

363.title: Honor, simply
363.hook: Epictetus on reverence: think rightly of the gods and keep offerings honest and plain (Enchiridion 31)
363.howItsDone: Epictetus advised keeping the customary offerings of one's ancestors, plainly and within one's means; some people on their own path today keep a small, simple ritual for whatever they hold sacred.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kathēkon, the fitting act, measured by the relationship. Your line was watch what you must do.

A small clay cup of wine, poured out on the ground before a meal. A handful of the first barley of the harvest, set at a household shrine. In Epictetus' world, offerings like these belonged to ordinary household life, the way some families today light a candle, say grace, or leave flowers at a grave. Section thirty-one of the handbook is about reverence, and what's striking is how little it asks for. Two things. Think rightly. Give plainly.
screen: `A CUP POURED ON THE GROUND.` → `THE FIRST BARLEY AT THE SHRINE.` → `HONOR, SIMPLY.`

segments.voice: First, the thinking. The most important part of piety, Epictetus says, is to hold right opinions about the gods: that they exist, and that they govern the whole well and justly. That's his belief, a Stoic's. People on their own path hold many different views here, and this lesson is about the shape of his advice more than his creed. Why the thinking matters: hold that view, he says, and you can follow what happens willingly, and never blame the gods. But only if you put good and bad in what's up to you. Put them in outside things, and every time you miss what you wanted, you'll feel cheated and resent whoever you think is in charge. His hard example comes from the old stories: Eteocles and Polynices, brothers who killed each other over the throne of Thebes, because each thought the crown was the good. Farmers, sailors and merchants complain at the sky for the same reason. Then the giving. Pour the libations, make the offerings, give the first fruits, he says, according to the custom of your ancestors. And do it purely. Not carelessly, not sloppily, not stingily, and not beyond what you can afford. You may not share his gods, or any gods. Still, a person can hold something sacred: a faith, the memory of a grandmother, a mountain, a quiet morning. His advice still fits. Don't make it a show, and don't let it go shabby. Honor it honestly, within your means, in the way you were given. Simple isn't the same as small.
screen: `FIRST: THINK RIGHTLY OF THE GODS.` · `MISPLACED GOOD BREEDS RESENTMENT.` · `NOT CARELESS, STINGY, OR TOO MUCH.` · `HONEST AND PLAIN, WHATEVER YOU HOLD.` · then, large: `HONESTLY, SIMPLY.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what you hold sacred: God, a tradition, a person who's gone, the sea, or something you have no name for. 364.title: No oracle needed
364.hook: ask diviners about things you can't know, never about whether to stand by a friend (Enchiridion 32)
364.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism separate questions about outcomes, which they may research or ask about, from questions about duty, which they try to answer by reason without waiting for a sign.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was honor: think rightly, give plainly, and keep it within your means. Your line was honestly, simply.

The call comes after midnight. A friend is in trouble, and they need someone to come. It's a moment when a small voice can start bargaining. Is this a good idea? Maybe I should sleep on it. People in Epictetus' day had a more formal way to stall. They went to a diviner, someone who read birds or the insides of a sacrifice, and asked what the gods advised. Epictetus doesn't mock the diviner. He just draws a line around what the diviner is for.
screen: `A FRIEND IN TROUBLE, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `ASK THE DIVINER?` → `NO ORACLE NEEDED.`

segments.voice: When you go to a diviner, Epictetus says, you don't know how things will turn out. That's why you came. But you do know what kind of thing it is. If it isn't up to you, it isn't good or bad in itself. So leave your craving and your dread at the door, and go in as you'd go to any adviser. When should you ask? The way Socrates did, he says: only when the whole question turns on what will happen, and reason and skill have nothing to offer. Will a voyage go well? Will a harvest come in? Questions like those, fine. When shouldn't you ask? When a friend or your country is in danger and you ought to share it, don't ask the diviner whether to. Even if the signs say death, injury or exile, reason has already answered. You stand by your friend. Then the greater diviner. Epictetus tells an old story about the god at Delphi, who, it was said, threw a man out of the temple because he had not helped a friend who was being killed. Even the oracle, in the story, sides with loyalty over omens. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: these things happen. Aim at the good. My mind is mine. First, what follows. What the role asks. Honestly, simply. And today: a duty doesn't wait for a sign.
screen: `LEAVE CRAVING AND DREAD AT THE DOOR.` · `ASK ONLY WHAT REASON CAN'T ANSWER.` · `A FRIEND IN DANGER? NO NEED TO ASK.` · `EVEN DELPHI SIDES WITH THE FRIEND.` · then, large: `NO ORACLE NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Think of one duty you've been putting off while you wait for some kind of sign: the right mood, a clearer feeling, someone else going first. Ask plainly whether it's a question about what will happen, or about what you owe. If it's what you owe, let the waiting go, and picture the first step.
Diviner. The adviser Epictetus says to consult only when reason has nothing to offer; when the question is whether to stand by a friend, reason has already answered. Today's word.
Your line: reason has already answered. A friend in trouble doesn't need an omen. Day three hundred sixty-four, and a week complete.
